images.alt: Find Your Future Machine Breakdown Mystery scenario and clues

texts: Think

Think of the last time a phone, bike, controller, or other item broke.

What was the FIRST thing you did to figure out what was wrong?
slides.lookFor: Students name an observation or first check before a repair.
slides.pivot: Offer turn it off/on, inspect damage, or ask what changed as starting examples.

texts: Troubleshooting

Do not guess and replace random parts.

Observe → identify → analyze → test one safe solution → prevent the next breakdown.
slides.lookFor: Students can explain why technicians gather evidence before changing the machine.
slides.pivot: Ask what could go wrong if a technician changes three parts at once.

texts: Machine Breakdown Mystery

YOU ARE THE TECHNICIAN
A fruit-packaging line has stopped. The label machine will not feed labels.

Production is at a standstill.
Your job: use the clues and the five-stage Technician Checklist to find the most defensible first repair.
slides.lookFor: Students understand the broken function: labels do not feed, while the rest of the line is running.
slides.pivot: Point to the exact machine and restate the production consequence.

texts: Technician Checklist: 1-2

1. IDENTIFY THE PROBLEM
What is not working? What happened right before it stopped?

2. ANALYZE POSSIBLE CAUSES
Mechanical failure? Electrical issue? Operator error? Something else?
slides.lookFor: Students separate the observed problem from possible causes.
slides.pivot: Model one observation and one hypothesis; do not solve the case yet.

texts: Technician Checklist: 3-5

3. Implement one safe solution
4. Test and observe
5. Prevent future breakdowns

If the test fails, return to the checklist with new evidence.
slides.lookFor: Students understand that testing can send the team back to an earlier step.
slides.pivot: Use a familiar broken-pencil-sharpener example if the loop is unclear.

texts: Read the Five Clues
Clicking noise • no smoke, sparks, or leaks • other machines still run • sticker roll is in place but labels do not feed • problem began after a new roll was installed

Circle the clue that narrows the cause most.
Underline what the clue rules out.
slides.lookFor: Students identify the newly installed roll as the strongest timing clue without treating it as proof.
slides.pivot: Ask: What changed right before the machine stopped?

texts: Pair Plan: Complete All Five Stages

Partner or private route:
1. Name the exact problem.
2. List two possible causes.
3. Choose one safe first solution.
4. Name the test result you need.
5. Prevent a repeat.

Do not jump from one clue to a final answer.
Your plan must show how the test proves or disproves the cause.
slides.lookFor: Every pair has evidence in Stage 1, a testable Stage 3 solution, and an observable Stage 4 result.
slides.pivot: At minute 24, stop one third of the class if they are writing repairs without causes.

texts: Likely first check
Best clue
Which clue narrowed the cause most?
Label-roll size, type, alignment, or jammed feed
Evidence Check
slides.lookFor: Students cite a clue and explain why it changes the first check.
slides.pivot: Clarify that likely is not confirmed; the controlled test supplies the next evidence.

images.alt: Find Your Future five-stage Technician Checklist

texts: Complete Model
Clue → cause → test

The problem began after a new label roll was installed. I would stop the machine, check the roll size and alignment, remove any jam, and run a short controlled test. If labels feed correctly, document the correct roll setup and add it to operator training.
slides.lookFor: Students can point to the clue, safe action, observable test, and prevention move.
slides.pivot: Read the model one sentence at a time and label each reasoning job.

texts: Choose One Hat

Return to Manufacturing in H&L.
Choose one Hat you noticed.
Keep that Hat open for research.
Different careers are welcome. Never force a student away from a real interest.
slides.lookFor: Each student has one actual Manufacturing career open, not only a cluster or pathway.
slides.pivot: Offer Welder, Automation Specialist, or Mechatronics Technician as fixed-source starting points.

texts: Research Six Fields

Career name
What interests you?
Brief job description
Education or training
Salary evidence
Tools, equipment, or skills
slides.lookFor: Students copy evidence from the Hat profile into the matching field without inventing missing details.
slides.pivot: Use the bilingual field labels or Welder example; reduce writing volume, not evidence quality.

texts: Label Salary Evidence

NUMBER OR RANGE
MEASURE
annual • hourly • monthly
GEOGRAPHY
local • Texas • U.S.

SOURCE + DATA YEAR OR DATE VIEWED
Keep H&L and BLS figures separate. A different national figure does not replace the district HQIM figure.
slides.lookFor: Salary entries include the number, measure, geography, source, and year/date.
slides.pivot: Project one correctly labeled sample and one unlabeled number; ask which is usable evidence.

texts: Exit: Recommend a Route

Jamie wants a Manufacturing job after high school.
1. Name one researched career.
2. Name two training or certification steps.
3. Estimate the total time.

Use your worksheet.
Do not promise admission, hiring, certification, or a local salary.
slides.lookFor: The recommendation uses the researched career and two concrete preparation steps with a defensible time estimate.
slides.pivot: Allow labeled bullets or speech-to-text; if training evidence is missing, students mark it to verify rather than guess.
